The root [根, ne] of Panax ginseng is described as a superior tonic drug [上品, jōhin] warming the five viscera [五臓, gozō], calming the spirit [安精神, an seishin], and supplementing depleted vital energy [補元気, ho genki].
results.translation: Ginseng (人参, Ninjin) is classified among the foremost tonic medicines, prized for warming the five viscera [五臓: heart, liver, spleen, lungs, kidneys] and stabilizing the spirit and mind. It is employed to replenish exhausted vital energy [元気, genki] and to restore those debilitated by chronic illness, old age, or constitutional weakness. Kaibara Ekiken notes that while Chinese medical tradition regards ginseng as universally applicable, Japanese physicians of his era exercised greater caution in its use, observing that the Japanese physical constitution [体質, taishitsu] may respond differently than the Chinese, and counseling restraint in cases involving heat excess [熱証, nesshō].

entities_mentioned.modern_identification: Panax ginseng C.A.Mey. (family Araliaceae)

Wild-harvested roots were considered superior to cultivated specimens.

results.translation: The root of the peony [芍薬, Shakuyaku] is recognized as a primary [君薬] blood-regulating drug in both Chinese and Japanese medical traditions; Kaibara Ekiken affirms its use for pacifying the blood [血を和す], relieving abdominal pain and cramping [腹痛・痙攣], and calming liver qi excess [肝気の亢進]. He further records that the plant was by his time cultivated widely across Japan's provinces for both ornamental and pharmaceutical purposes, and he cautions that the raw root differs in action from the root prepared by boiling [湯煮], the latter being milder and more appropriate for deficient constitutions [虚証].

results.translation: Cinnamon bark [桂皮, Keihi] is classified among the warm and acrid medicinal woods, prized in Japanese practice for its ability to dispel cold, invigorate the circulation of blood and vital energy [気, ki], and warm the interior organs, particularly the stomach and kidneys. The bark was regarded as especially effective in cases of cold-type abdominal pain, deficiency of yang [陽虚, yō-kyo], and sluggish digestion, reflecting the broader Edo-period adaptation of Chinese medical theory [漢方, Kanpō] to Japanese clinical experience.
